titleFa: کتاب The Heart of the Matter
author: Graham Greene
introFa: کتاب «The Heart of the Matter» نوشته Graham Greene یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Heart of the Matter»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: INVITED COMMENTARY Anthracyclines and trastuzumab; getting to the heart of the matter: when getting to the heart is the matter Patrick G. Morris Æ Clifford A. Hudis Received: 7 August 2008 / Accepted: 25 August 2008 / Published online: 13 September 2008  Springer Science+Business Media, LLC. 2008 Background Despite expanding treatment options, anthracyclines remain among the most active chemotherapeutic agents for breast cancer. In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer (MBC) the pivotal phase III study by Slamon et al. dem- onstrated that the addition of trastuzumab to chemotherapy improved the median time to disease progression from 4.6 to 7.4 months [1]. The addition of trastuzumab to anthra- cyclines (doxorubicin or epirubicin given once every 3 weeks) increased the rate of all grades of cardiac failure from 8% to 27% [2]. Following the publication of these data trastuzumab has not been routinely administered concurrently with anthracycline-based chemotherapy, and adjuvant studies have utilized a sequential approach. In order to ‘‘improve the therapeutic index of anthracycline/ trastuzumab combinations’’ in MBC Gennari et al. designed a phase II study, published in the current issue of this journal, and discussed in this commentary. In this study patients with HER2-positive MBC were treated with epirubicin 90 mg/m2 every 3 weeks in combination with so-called weekly ‘‘low-dose’’ trastuzumab (2 mg/kg load- ing dose then 1 mg/kg) [3]. Trastuzumab dosing The most striking aspect of the design of this study is the trastuzumab dose used, which is only half the current standard. In the development of trastuzumab phase II studies sought to achieve serum concentrations greater than 10 lg/ml, a level which had been associated with optimal inhibition of cell growth in a preclinical model [4]. Both the weekly dosing schedule (4 mg/kg loading dose and 2 mg/kg maintenance) and the 3 weekly schedule (8 mg/kg loading and 6 mg/kg maintenance) achieved steady-state concentrations in the region of 60 lg/ml [5, 6]. As noted by Gennari et al. this clearly exceeds the required pre-clinical threshold. The ﬁrst phase II study of trastuzumab had actually used weekly ﬁxed dosing (250 mg loading and 100 mg maintenance) and also achieved adequate serum concentration ([10 lg/ml) in 90% of patients [7]. For many patients this dosing schedule represents a slightly lower total trastuzumab dose. Theoretically lower trast- uzumab doses as used by Gennari et al. could still ensure therapeutic serum levels. However there is a lack of pharmacokinetic data from the current study and elsewhere to correlate the ‘‘low dose’’ schedule with serum trast- uzumab concentration. In addition there are no data comparing the clinical outcome of patients treated with conventionally scheduled trastuzumab to the proposed ‘‘low-dose’’. Such studies are unlikely to be carried out. Cardiac toxicity of trastuzumab in MBC The cardiac toxicity of trastuzumab is poorly understood, partly due to the lack of an animal model and dearth of cardiac biopsies in humans [8]. It initially was thought to be similar to the cardiomyopathy seen with anthracyclines, but appears to be less severe and more easily reversible. As Gennari et al. point out the relationship between dose of trastuzumab and cardiac toxicity is not well established which causes us to question what evidence is there that the This is a commentary to doi:10.1007/s10549-008-0048-8. lower trastuzumab dosing in the current study would be expected to result in less cardiac failure? The risk of cardiac toxicity with trastuzumab, while real, is relatively rare, appears to be reversible and treatable in many cases, and must be balanced against the potentially substantial beneﬁts of trastuzumab therapy in particular for incurable metastatic disease. Very few cardiac deaths have been linked to trastuzumab and many patients with pre- existing cardiac dysfunction or who develop cardiac failure on trastuzumab are able to continue treatment. While there are no validated screening and treatment algorithms for trastuzumab-induced cardiomyopathy clinical trials have tended to adjust therapy based on changes in left ventric- ular ejection fraction (LVEF). The importance of this monitoring, particularly in asymptomatic patients with MBC is not well established and an individualized approach is needed. Combination of anthracycline and trastuzumab The current study examines an anthracycline and trast- uzumab in a patient subpopulation that is probably diminishing (taxane and trastuzumab naı¨ve) as many patients now receive adjuvant therapy with anthracyclines, taxanes and trastuzumab. If there are such patients, the combination of an anthracycline with the use of low-dose trastuzumab and full-dose epirubicin may be a sub-optimal option. Full-dose (standard) trastuzumab with modiﬁed anthracycline dosing and scheduling could be a less toxic option since the risk of cardiac toxicity is more clearly linked to cumulative anthracycline exposure. For example, weekly epirubicin (25 mg/m2) has been studied as mono- therapy in pretreated patients and/or those with a low performance status and shown to be both active and well tolerated [9]. An earlier phase I study combining epirubicin and cyclophosphamide with trastuzumab showed a high rate of asymptomatic decline in LVEF [ 10%, which occurred in 48% (epirubicin 60 mg/m2 and trastuzumab), 56% (epiru- bicin 90 mg/m2 and trastuzumab) and only 24% (epirubicin 90 mg/m2 without trastuzumab) [10]. All these patients were anthracycline-naı¨ve. Gennari and colleagues report that in the current study eight episodes of protocol deﬁned cardiotoxicity were observed: six patients (13.6%) showed a decline in LVEF [ 15% from baseline, while maintain- ing an absolute LVEF greater than 50% and two patients (4.5%) developed symptomatic cardiac failure after a median cumulative epirubicin dose of 720 mg/m2: neither of these patients had received adjuvant anthracyclines. Conclusion Combining anthracyclines and trastuzumab is not a stan- dard therapeutic approach in HER2-positive MBC. Patients pre-treated with adjuvant anthracyclines are generally treated with taxane-trastuzumab combinations in the ﬁrst- line metastatic setting as per the Slamon study [1]. While the investigational regimen used by Gennari et al. is associated with similar (albeit non-randomized) response rates to the Slamon study the associated cardiac toxicity is signiﬁcant as described making this less desirable for fur- ther study or clinical use.
